Table 1 gives Human / GPT-3 / Collaborative / Total idea counts: Team 1, 20 / 4 / 2 / 26; Team 2, 18 / 11 / 11 / 40; Team 3, 17 / 2 / 0 / 19; Team 4, 24 / 6 / 6 / 36; Team 5, 18 / 6 / 3 / 27. The accompanying text gives average word counts of 16.5 for Human-Generated ideas and 20.9 for GPT-3-Generated ideas. Record these as descriptive fluency and elaboration measures; the counts are ideas, not people, and the fixed phases do not provide a randomized assistance contrast.

corrections.source_says: The form mentions independent output scoring in its summary and eligibility reason but does not record those outcomes. The paper evaluates 148 ideas, using 3 expert reviewers, 6 novice reviewers, and GPT-4, on relevance, innovation, and insightfulness. Table 4 reports Average over all ideas, Avg / Stdev, as follows: Expert relevance 3.57 / 1.10, innovation 2.79 / 1.10, insightfulness 3.01 / 1.11; Novice relevance 3.38 / 0.95, innovation 3.11 / 1.07, insightfulness 3.13 / 0.96; GPT-4 relevance 4.19 / 0.82, innovation 3.72 / 0.80, insightfulness 3.68 / 0.80. Record the descriptive output scores and the 148-idea corpus separately from the 16 idea-generating students. These summaries pool human, GPT-3, and collaborative ideas and compare evaluators; they are not estimates of an AI-assistance effect. Do not substitute 148 for the number of people or for the unknown number of student self-ratings.
corrections.quote: We compare the ratings given GPT-4 to those given by novices and experts to the 148 ideas generated by either humans, GPT-3, or in collaboration.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 17, sections 5.3 and 5.3.2; p. 18, Figure 5 and section 5.3.2(a); p. 20, Table 4, Average over all ideas column

corrections.source_says: The diversity-method fields are blank despite methods being reported. The analysis aggregates the five Conceptboards, extracts nouns and adjectives with spaCy, and uses GPT-4 for semantic analysis. Semantic cluster counts and shared terms compare the pooled Human-Generated and GPT-3-Generated idea sources, not pairs of different participants or randomized arms. No embedding model or uncertainty estimate for the cluster-count comparison is specified. The accompanying LPA analysis compares normalized term-frequency distributions with symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence and identifies overused, underused, or missing terms; Figure 4 reports that analysis. Describe these methods and retain question=none for this source-pool comparison; full cluster lists are in the separately cited Supplementary Information.
corrections.quote: GPT-4 was used for Semantic Analysis, and Python was used for descriptive analysis and LPA.
corrections.locator: PDF pp. 11-12, section 5.1 and Equation 1; pp. 14-15, section 5.2.3; p. 16, Figure 4

corrections.source_says: The paper explicitly mentions a separate report about integration of the framework into the tangible interaction course and students' reflections and learning. Record this as a possible overlapping course/sample report instead of leaving the overlap note empty. The passage identifies it only as a paper then under review for a different conference; its bibliographic identity and exact participant overlap are not confirmed here.
corrections.quote: In a separate paper [currently under review for a different conference], we contextualized the use of this framework within a broader integration of generative AI into a tangible interaction course, and discussed students’ reflections and learning.

confirmed: Source version, title, and author list match the local PDF: arXiv:2402.14978v2, 29 Feb 2024; the file has 27 pages (PDF p. 1 version stamp and title block; final page p. 27). The complete 699-line markdown was read, including the references; no appendix or supplementary section follows them.

No randomized human AI-assistance study is reported. Everyone generated ideas independently, then co-created and developed ideas with GPT-3 in the same fixed order; quasi_people and observational context are appropriate (PDF p. 8, section 4; pp. 9-10, section 4.1).

The study involved 16 college students, 0 men, ages 18-23, in a 70-minute session, divided into five project teams. All 16 answered the immediate reflection question; the participant cohort is below 50, and the repeated phases are not separate samples to be added together (PDF p. 8, section 4.1; p. 9, section 4.1; p. 12, section 5.2.1). No count of people randomized is reported because no AI-assistance assignment was randomized.

Random order refers to presentation of ideas to raters, not allocation of people to AI assistance. Four expert reviewers were recruited, but results report the three who rated all ideas, together with six novice reviewers; they are separate evaluators, not additional idea-generating participants (PDF p. 11, section 5.1).

S1-O1 reported and one_line_finding correctly reproduce innovation self-ratings: Collab Avg 4.81, Std 0.40; Human Avg 4.31, Std 0.70. These are descriptive student self-ratings, and no inferential assistance-effect test accompanies this comparison (PDF p. 10, section 4.2 and Table 2).

S1-O2 reported correctly gives 20 semantic clusters for Human-Generated ideas, 21 for GPT-3-Generated ideas, and 12 similar clusters containing shared terms. These compare source pools, not diversity between randomized groups of people (PDF pp. 14-15, section 5.2.3).

GPT-3 via OpenAI Playground supported the ideation session; GPT-4 evaluated ideas after the final-idea selection deadline, and these evaluations were unavailable to the students during ideation (PDF p. 9, section 4.1; p. 17, section 5.3; p. 20, section 5.3.3).

Actual output scoring is present independently of the student self-ratings: expert, novice, and GPT-4 evaluations cover relevance, innovation, and insightfulness. Thus criterion 3 is met, while lack of random assignment and fewer than 50 participants support core=no (PDF p. 17, section 5.3; pp. 8-9, sections 4-4.1).

Supplementary Information is cited for the evaluation prompt and scale explanations and for full semantic-cluster term lists, but is not included in this PDF (PDF p. 8, section 3.3; p. 15, section 5.2.3; PDF ends with references on p. 27).

This is an empirical course study with subsequent evaluations of its idea corpus, not a synthesis; leaving synthesis study counts and pooled estimates empty is appropriate (PDF pp. 8-20, sections 4-5).
summary: The form correctly identifies a nonrandomized study of 16 students, and its source version, reported statistics, and one-line finding match the PDF. Five corrections document omitted outcome scores and output counts, diversity-method details, and a possible overlapping report.
